claims.text: The as-deposited protective coating is a dual-phase HEA containing uniformly distributed FCC and BCC domains.
Deposition or post-processing parameters can be adjusted to vary the spacing and density of FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
Reduced FCC/BCC domain spacing increases interphase-boundary density.
Creep deformation is activated during sustained loading at service-relevant elevated temperatures.
FCC/BCC interphase boundaries impede dislocation motion.
FCC/BCC interphase boundaries induce dislocation pile-ups.
A higher density of closely spaced FCC/BCC interfaces increases the frequency of dislocation blockage.
More frequent dislocation blockage reduces the rate of plastic deformation under continuous load.
Reducing FCC/BCC interphase spacing enhances creep resistance.
Samples with reduced interphase spacing will have lower creep rates than the as-deposited baseline.
Samples with increased interphase spacing will have higher creep rates than the as-deposited baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies in creep regimes where interphase-controlled dislocation interactions dominate other hardening mechanisms.
Thermally activated dislocation climb may also contribute to creep behavior.
Changing deposition conditions may introduce secondary microstructural changes that affect creep behavior.
A controlled series of coatings with varied interphase spacing can be compared under identical sustained loading and temperature.
The hypothesis is falsified if creep strain rate does not vary significantly with interphase spacing or if reduced-spacing samples do not consistently outperform the baseline.
